newsitem.title: INDIA: Union chief's death puts focus on Bombay land crisis.
newsitem.headline: Union chief's death puts focus on Bombay land crisis.

text.p: The slaying of a prominent trade union chief in a hail of bullets has thrown a spotlight on organised crime and the soaring price of real estate in India's commercial capital, Bombay.
Land prices in the city are among the highest in the world with prime sites in desperately short supply, due to a combination of archaic rent laws and landholding restrictions.
Datta Samant, 65, a powerful union firebrand who made the city's cotton textile mill owners cringe and won workers' hearts, was shot dead by four unidentified gunmen in a Bombay suburb on Thursday.
Trade unions called a general strike to protest the mafia- style killing.
For several years, Bombay's mill owners have battled thousands of workers as they sought to move their operations out of the prime real estate in the heart of the crowded city.

"Of the 54 mills in Bombay, only about 15 managements are genuinely interested in running their units. The others would rather be real estate agents," Govindrao Adik, the leader of the Rashtriya Mill Mazdoor Sangh (RMMS) union, said recently.

The mills whose chimneys dot the city's skyline offer the only new space to expand. Spread over 500 acres (200 hectares), they are collectively estimated to be worth more than 150 billion rupees ($4.2 billion).
The labourers who work there for a pittance have become pawns in a high-stakes game involving builders, landsharks and industrialists.

It is a game punctuated with dozens of gangland-style deaths. In May 1994, Sunit Khatau, whose family owns one of Bombay's largest mills, was shot dead when his car stopped at traffic lights in a killing that mirrored Thursday's attack.
Police and labour unions say Samant, a former member of parliament, may have been the victim of gangland rivalry.

"We cannot rule out the chance that some underworld gang was paid to eliminate him," said senior police officer R.S. Sharma, leading the investigation. "We have to check all the possibilities before we can say with certainty."
Before his death, Samant had led the labourers in an often bitter struggle against proprietors, who found themselves unable to shut down mills.
"Samant has filed several cases against the management of mills to prevent them from evicting workers from the premises where they live," a union official told Reuters.
The Congress-led RMMS union is a rival of Samant's Kamgar Aghadi, or Workers' Front political party, formed to protect the interests of the workers he led for over two decades.
Samant's unions command nearly one million workers spread over more than 4,000 factories in and around Bombay and in other parts of Maharashtra.

As hundreds of thousands of distraught workers gathered for Samant's funeral on Friday, a union official told Reuters there could have been several motives for the murder, as Samant had made many enemies during the last 30 years.
"Not a single piece of land owned by textile mills was sold between 1984 and 1989 when Samant was a member of parliament," said the official, who asked not to be identified.
